What is Docker: Containerization platform that packages applications with their complete dependencies into isolated units called containers.
Containers vs Images: Images are read-only blueprints; containers are runnable, isolated instances created from those blueprints.
Docker Architecture: Docker uses a client-server architecture with a CLI communicating via REST API to a daemon (dockerd) that manages images, containers, networks, and volumes.

# Components:
# Client (docker CLI) -> REST API -> Dockerd (daemon) -> containerd -> runc
# dockerd: high-level management
# containerd: container lifecycle
# runc: OCI runtime (spawns containers)
Docker Desktop: Desktop application for macOS, Windows, and Linux that includes Docker Engine, Docker CLI, Docker Compose, Kubernetes, and a GUI management dashboard.

# Docker Desktop includes:
# - Docker Engine + CLI
# - Docker Compose
# - Built-in Kubernetes
# - Extensions marketplace
# - Dev Environments
# - Resource management UI
WSL2 Backend: On Windows, Docker Desktop can run the Linux kernel inside a lightweight WSL2 VM for native Linux container performance without Hyper-V.

# Enable WSL2 backend in Docker Desktop Settings > Resources > WSL Integration
# Then run:
docker run --rm -it ubuntu bash
Daemon Configuration: Dockerd behavior is configured via daemon.json, controlling storage driver, log driver, registry mirrors, insecure registries, and resource limits.
docker info: Display system-wide information about the Docker installation, including OS, storage driver, CPUs, memory, and running container counts.
Lifecycle Management: Create, launch, stop, and clean up container runtimes explicitly through Docker commands.

docker run -d --name app nginx
docker stop app
docker rm app
Listing & Inspecting: List running containers with docker ps, all containers with -a, and view detailed metadata with docker inspect.

docker ps
docker ps -a
docker inspect app

Dockerfile Basics: Instruction set for creating container images. Each instruction creates a layer in the final image.

FROM alpine:3.19
RUN apk add --no-cache nodejs
COPY app.js .
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
FROM Variants: Choose base images wisely: alpine (5MB), slim (Debian minimal), distroless (language runtime only), or scratch (empty) for different size and security trade-offs.

FROM alpine:3.19          # 5MB, musl libc
FROM node:20-slim         # Debian minimal
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20   # 120MB, no shell
FROM scratch              # truly empty
RUN Layers: Each RUN instruction creates a new layer. Chain commands with && and clean up in the same layer to reduce image size.

# BAD: three layers
RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y curl
RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# GOOD: single layer
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y curl && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY vs ADD: COPY copies files from context into the image. ADD does the same plus supports remote URLs and auto-extracting tar archives. Prefer COPY unless you need ADD's extras.

COPY ./app /app              # simple, preferred
COPY --chown=node:node . /app
ADD https://example.com/file.tar.gz /tmp/   # ADD supports URLs
ADD archive.tar.gz /tmp/                    # ADD auto-extracts
ARG vs ENV: ARG defines build-time variables (not in final image unless persisted). ENV defines runtime environment variables that persist in the final image.

ARG NODE_VERSION=20
FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}
ARG BUILD_ENV              # build only: --build-arg BUILD_ENV=prod
ENV NODE_ENV=production    # persists in image
WORKDIR: Sets the working directory for all subsequent Dockerfile instructions (RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY, ADD). Creates the directory if it does not exist.

FROM node:20
WORKDIR /app               # all subsequent commands run here
COPY package.json .        # copies to /app/package.json
RUN npm install
USER: Switch to a non-root user for better security. Always create a dedicated user; never run containers as root unless absolutely necessary.

FROM node:20-slim
RUN groupadd -r app && useradd -r -g app app
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN chown -R app:app /app
USER app
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
EXPOSE: Documents which ports the container listens on at runtime. It is documentation only — does not publish the port. Use -p or -P at runtime to publish.

FROM nginx
EXPOSE 80                   # documents port 80
EXPOSE 443/tcp              # can specify protocol
# docker run -p 8080:80 nginx to actually publish
LABEL: Add metadata as key-value pairs to the image. Used for versioning, maintainer info, and organization. Use with --filter for image queries.

FROM alpine
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.title="myapp"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.version="1.0.0"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.vendor="Acme Corp"
# Query: docker images --filter label=org.opencontainers.image.vendor=Acme
SHELL: Override the default shell (Linux: /bin/sh, Windows: cmd) used by RUN instructions. Useful for Windows containers or custom shells.

FROM alpine
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]    # default is /bin/sh
RUN echo "using bash now"

# Windows example:
# SHELL ["powershell", "-Command"]
HEALTHCHECK: Tells Docker how to test if the container is working. Docker checks the command periodically; exits with 0 = healthy, 1 = unhealthy.
Multi-Stage Build: Use multiple FROM statements to chain build environments. Copy only required artifacts to the final stage, drastically reducing image size.

FROM golang:1.22 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app/server

FROM alpine:3.19
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates
COPY --from=builder /app/server /server
CMD ["/server"]
BuildKit: Modern Docker build backend (enabled by default in newer versions) with parallel builds, secrets mounting, SSH mounts, and better caching.

# Enable BuildKit (default in Docker 23+)
export DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1

# Build with secrets (no secret in image layers)
# docker build --secret id=mysecret,src=./secret.txt .
# RUN --mount=type=secret,id=mysecret cat /run/secrets/mysecret
Buildx: Extended build capabilities built on BuildKit. Enables multi-architecture builds, simultaneous builds for linux/amd64, linux/arm64, etc.

docker buildx create --name mybuilder --use
docker buildx inspect --bootstrap

# Build for multiple architectures
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64,linux/arm/v7 \
  -t myapp:latest --push .
Cache Mounts: Persist package manager caches across builds using BuildKit cache mounts, speeding up repeated RUN instructions significantly.

FROM node:20
WORKDIR /app

# Cache npm packages across builds
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci --only=production

# Cache apt packages
# RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt \
#     apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3
.dockerignore: Prevent unnecessary files from being sent to the Docker daemon during builds, reducing context size and improving build speed.

docker run deep: The primary command to create and start containers. Supports --name, --rm (auto-remove on exit), --restart, -d (detach), --network, and many more flags.
Interactive Mode: Run containers interactively with -it (--interactive + --tty) for shell access, debugging, or one-off commands.

docker run -it --rm alpine /bin/sh
# Inside container:
# / # apk add curl
# / # exit
Detachment: Run containers in the background with -d flag. Re-attach with docker attach, or follow logs with docker logs -f.

docker run -d --name redis redis:alpine
docker attach redis          # attaches to STDOUT/STDERR
Ctrl+P Ctrl+Q               # detach without stopping
Resource Limits: Constrain container CPU, memory, and disk I/O using --memory, --cpus, --memory-swap, and --blkio-weight flags.
Logging Drivers: Configure how containers send logs. Drivers: json-file (default), syslog, journald, gelf, fluentd, awslogs, gcplogs, and local (efficient).

docker run --log-driver=local --log-opt max-size=10m nginx
docker run --log-driver=syslog --log-opt syslog-address=udp://192.168.1.1:514 nginx
# daemon.json default: "log-driver": "json-file"
Restart Policies: Control automatic container restarts: no (never), always, on-failure[:max-retries], unless-stopped (also restarts after daemon restart).

docker run --restart no              # never restart (default)
docker run --restart always           # always restart
docker run --restart on-failure:5     # restart on error, max 5 times
docker run --restart unless-stopped   # restart unless manually stopped
stop vs kill: docker stop sends SIGTERM (graceful shutdown, 10s timeout), then SIGKILL. docker kill sends any signal (default SIGKILL) immediately.

docker stop --time=30 app      # SIGTERM + 30s timeout
docker kill app                  # immediate SIGKILL
docker kill -s HUP app           # send SIGHUP (reload config)
update: Dynamically update container resource constraints, restart policy, and other configuration on a running container without recreating it.

docker update --memory=1g --cpus=2 app
docker update --restart=always app
rename: Rename a running or stopped container without affecting its internal state, IP, or volumes.

docker run -d --name oldname nginx
docker rename oldname newname
wait: Block the shell until a container stops, then return its exit code. Useful for scripting and CI pipelines.

docker run -d --name job busybox sh -c "exit 42"
docker wait job
# Output: 42
Port Mapping Deep: Map container ports to the host with -p (specific) or -P (random ephemeral ports). Supports IPv4/IPv6, multiple protocols, and ranges.

docker run -p 8080:80/tcp nginx              # TCP only
docker run -p 192.168.1.1:8080:80 nginx      # bind to specific IP
docker run -p 80:80 -p 443:443 nginx         # multiple ports
docker run -P nginx                          # random ports
Environment Variables: Pass configuration via -e flags, --env-file, or ENV instructions in Dockerfile. Variables are isolated per container.

docker run -e DB_HOST=localhost -e DB_PORT=5432 app
docker run --env-file .env app
# Inside: echo $DB_HOST

Port Forwarding: Map isolated internal container ports onto host interfaces, enabling external access to containerized services.
DNS Resolution: Containers on user-defined bridges resolve each other by container name or network alias. Docker embeds a DNS server at 127.0.0.11.

docker network create mynet
docker run --network mynet --name web nginx
docker run --network mynet alpine ping web   # resolves by name
Network Drivers Deep: bridge (default, NAT), host (no isolation), overlay (multi-host), macvlan (MAC per container), ipvlan (IP per container), none (isolated).

# bridge: default, NAT'd, containers communicate via IP/name
# host: shares host network stack, no port mapping needed
# none: loopback only, fully isolated
# overlay: swarm multi-host, requires key-value store
# macvlan: assign real MAC from physical network
User-Defined Bridge: Create custom bridge networks for automatic DNS resolution, network isolation between groups, and attach/detach containers dynamically.

docker network create --driver bridge --subnet 172.20.0.0/16 mynet
docker network connect mynet container1
docker network disconnect mynet container1
docker network inspect mynet
Host Network: Remove network isolation to run directly on the host's network stack. No port mapping needed; container sees host interfaces.

docker run -d --network host nginx
# Access at http://localhost:80 directly
# No -p flag needed
Macvlan: Assign a real MAC address to each container, making them appear as physical devices on the network. Useful for legacy apps that require direct network access.

docker network create -d macvlan \
  --subnet=192.168.1.0/24 \
  --gateway=192.168.1.1 \
  -o parent=eth0 \
  my-macvlan

docker run --network my-macvlan --ip=192.168.1.100 nginx
Ipvlan: Assign IP addresses to containers sharing the host's MAC address. L2 mode (same subnet) and L3 mode (routing between subnets) supported.

docker network create -d ipvlan \
  --subnet=10.0.0.0/24 \
  -o parent=eth0 \
  -o ipvlan_mode=l2 \
  my-ipvlan
Network Aliases: Give a container multiple DNS names within a network. Useful for running multiple variants of the same service.

docker run --network mynet --network-alias api-v1 --network-alias api-v2 nginx
# Both api-v1 and api-v2 resolve to this container on mynet
Container Networking Model: Docker's CNM defines Sandbox (namespace), Endpoint (veth pair), and Network (bridge/overlay) as core primitives for container networking.

# Sandbox: network namespace (isolated stack)
# Endpoint: veth pair connecting sandbox to network
# Network: group of endpoints (bridge, overlay, etc.)
# libnetwork implements CNM
Overlay Networks: Multi-host networks that span across Docker swarm nodes, enabling container communication across different hosts securely over VXLAN.

docker network create --driver overlay --attachable my-overlay
docker service create --network my-overlay --name web --replicas 3 nginx

Named Volumes: Persistent data directories managed by Docker, isolated from container lifecycle. Survive container removal and can be shared across containers.

docker volume create mydata
docker run -v mydata:/data alpine echo "stored"
docker volume ls
docker volume inspect mydata
docker volume rm mydata
Bind Mounts: Mount a host file or directory into a container at a specific path. Changes are reflected instantly on both sides.

docker run -v /host/path:/container/path nginx
# Short form: -v $(pwd)/src:/app/src
# Long form: --mount type=bind,source=$(pwd)/src,target=/app/src
tmpfs Mounts: Mount a temporary filesystem stored in memory (RAM), not on disk. Data is lost when the container stops. Ideal for secrets or cache.
Storage Drivers: Manage image layers and container writable layers. overlay2 (default, modern), aufs (legacy), devicemapper, btrfs, zfs, vfs.

# overlay2 (default, recommended)
# - Union mount of layers
# - Copy-on-write
# - Best performance, lowest overhead
# Check: docker info | grep "Storage Driver"
Volume Drivers: Plugins that extend Docker volumes to remote storage systems: NFS, SSHFS, S3, Azure File, Google Cloud, REX-Ray, Portworx.

docker volume create --driver vieux/sshfs \
  -o sshcmd=user@host:/remote/path \
  -o password=secret \
  sshvolume

docker run -v sshvolume:/data alpine
Backup & Restore Volumes: Back up volume data using a temporary container that mounts the volume and creates a tar archive.

# Backup
docker run --rm -v mydata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/mydata-backup.tar.gz -C /data .

# Restore
docker run --rm -v mydata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine \
  tar xzf /backup/mydata-backup.tar.gz -C /data
Bind Mount Deep: Bind mounts can be read-only, create missing host paths automatically, and support SELinux relabeling with :Z or :z suffixes.

docker run -v $(pwd):/app:ro nginx               # read-only
docker run -v $(pwd):/app:z nginx                # shared SELinux
docker run -v $(pwd):/app:Z nginx                # private SELinux
# Long form:
docker run --mount type=bind,source=$(pwd),target=/app,readonly nginx
Permissions: Container processes run as root by default, creating files owned by root on bind-mounted directories. Use --user or USER to match host UID/GID.

# Run with host user's UID/GID
docker run --user $(id -u):$(id -g) -v $(pwd):/app alpine touch /app/test.txt

# Or set ownership in Dockerfile
COPY --chown=node:node . /app

Compose File Structure: YAML file defining services, networks, and volumes for multi-container applications. Version 3 targets Swarm; version 2 targets single-engine.

services:
  web:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "80:80"
    networks:
      - frontend
  api:
    build: ./api
    networks:
      - frontend
      - backend
networks:
  frontend: {}
  backend: {}
volumes:
  data: {}
Profiles: Selectively start services with --profile. Services only start when their profile is activated, enabling different environments (dev, test, staging).

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres
  adminer:
    image: adminer
    profiles: ["tools"]       # only with --profile tools
  mailhog:
    image: mailhog/mailhog
    profiles: ["debug", "tools"]

# docker compose --profile tools up
Extends: Inherit and override service definitions from another Compose file or within the same file, reducing duplication across environments.

# base.yml
services:
  web:
    image: nginx
    ports: ["80:80"]

# override.yml (extends merges configs)
services:
  web:
    extends:
      file: base.yml
      service: web
    environment:
      - NODE_ENV=production
depends_on Deep: Control startup order between services. Supports condition: service_started, service_healthy (requires healthcheck), or service_completed_successfully.

services:
  api:
    build: ./api
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      migrations:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-U", "postgres"]
  migrations:
    build: ./migrations
Healthcheck in Compose: Define container health checks in Compose. Automatically used by depends_on condition: service_healthy and by Swarm for rolling updates.

services:
  web:
    image: nginx
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 10s
env_file: Load environment variables from one or more files. Supports multiple env_file entries; values are available to the container at runtime.

services:
  app:
    image: node:20
    env_file:
      - ./common.env
      - ./secrets.env    # keep out of version control
    # Or inline:
    environment:
      - NODE_ENV=production
Secrets in Compose: Manage sensitive data (passwords, API keys, certificates) using Docker secrets. Mounted as files at /run/secrets/ inside the container.

services:
  app:
    image: myapp
    secrets:
      - db_password
      - tls_cert

secrets:
  db_password:
    file: ./db_password.txt
  tls_cert:
    external: true    # pre-created with docker secret create
Configs in Compose: Manage non-sensitive configuration files (config files, nginx conf, etc.) similar to secrets. Mounted at the specified target path.

services:
  nginx:
    image: nginx:alpine
    configs:
      - source: nginx_conf
        target: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
      - source: ssl_cert
        target: /etc/nginx/ssl/cert.pem

configs:
  nginx_conf:
    file: ./nginx/default.conf
  ssl_cert:
    external: true
Deploy Section: Swarm-only deployment configuration: replicas, update config, rollback config, restart_policy, placement constraints, resources, and endpoint mode.

services:
  web:
    image: nginx
    deploy:
      replicas: 5
      update_config:
        parallelism: 2
        delay: 10s
        order: start-first
      rollback_config:
        parallelism: 1
        order: stop-first
      restart_policy:
        condition: on-failure
        max_attempts: 3
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.5"
          memory: 256M
      placement:
        constraints: [node.role == worker]
Compose Watch: Automatically update running containers when source files change (Compose 2.22+). Supports sync, rebuild, and restart actions.

services:
  app:
    image: node:20
    develop:
      watch:
        - action: sync
          path: ./src
          target: /app/src
        - action: rebuild
          path: package.json

# docker compose up --watch

Swarm Init: Initialize a Docker Swarm cluster, transforming the host into a manager node. Swarm manages services across multiple hosts.

docker swarm init --advertise-addr 192.168.1.10
# Outputs join tokens for workers and managers
Node Types: Managers run the control plane and Raft consensus (odd count recommended). Workers run only tasks. Nodes can be promoted or demoted.

# Add worker: docker swarm join --token WORKER_TOKEN
docker node ls
docker node promote node2
docker node demote node1
docker node update --availability drain node3
Raft Consensus: Swarm uses the Raft algorithm to maintain a consistent cluster state across manager nodes. Requires at least 3 managers for high availability.

# Best practice: 3 or 5 managers
# Raft tolerates (n-1)/2 failures
# 3 managers -> tolerate 1 failure
# 5 managers -> tolerate 2 failures
# docker swarm init --force-new-cluster (recover)
Service Replication: Deploy replicated services across Swarm nodes with --replicas. Docker schedules tasks evenly across available nodes.

docker service create --replicas 3 --name web -p 80:80 nginx
docker service scale web=5
docker service ps web
Rolling Updates: Update services incrementally with controlled parallelism and delay. Supports automatic rollback on failure and health check gate.

docker service update --image nginx:1.25 --update-parallelism 2 --update-delay 30s web
# Or in Compose deploy.update_config
Secrets Deep: Encrypted secrets stored in the Swarm Raft store. Only granted services can access them. Mounted as tmpfs files at /run/secrets/.

echo "mypassword" | docker secret create db_pass -
docker service create --secret db_pass --name db postgres
# Inside container: cat /run/secrets/db_pass
# Secrets are encrypted at rest and in transit
Configs in Swarm: Similar to secrets but for non-sensitive config files. Configs are stored in the Swarm Raft store and mounted into containers.

docker config create nginx_conf ./default.conf
docker service create --config src=nginx_conf,target=/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf --name web nginx
docker stack: Deploy a complete Compose application to Swarm as a stack. Stack name prefixes all service names for isolation.

docker stack deploy -c docker-compose.yml myapp
docker stack ls
docker stack services myapp
docker stack ps myapp
docker stack rm myapp
Swarm Mode Networking: Swarm uses ingress overlay network for routing mesh, and can attach services to custom overlay networks for multi-host communication.

# Ingress network: routes published ports to any node
docker network create --driver overlay --subnet 10.0.10.0/24 my-overlay
docker service create --network my-overlay --name api nginx
Routing Mesh: Swarm's routing mesh allows any node in the cluster to accept traffic on published ports and route it to a container on any other node.

# Publish port 80 on all Swarm nodes
# Traffic to any node:80 -> routed to a healthy container
docker service create --name web --publish published=80,target=80 --replicas 5 nginx
# curl http://any-swarm-node:80

Seccomp Profiles: Linux syscall filter (Secure Computing Mode) that restricts which system calls a container can make. Docker ships a default seccomp profile allowing ~300 of ~450 syscalls.

docker run --security-opt seccomp=default.json nginx
# Custom profile: allow specific syscalls only
docker run --security-opt seccomp=custom-profile.json nginx
# Disable seccomp (not recommended):
# docker run --security-opt seccomp=unconfined nginx
AppArmor: Mandatory Access Control (MAC) system that confines programs to a limited set of resources. Docker generates and loads an AppArmor profile for containers by default.

docker run --security-opt apparmor=docker-default nginx
# Load custom profile:
# apparmor_parser -r custom-profile
# docker run --security-opt apparmor=custom-profile nginx
Linux Capabilities: Fine-grained privileges for container processes. Drop all capabilities with --cap-drop=all, then add only required ones. Avoid --privileged.

docker run --cap-drop=ALL --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE nginx
# Common capabilities to add:
# NET_BIND_SERVICE: bind to privileged ports (<1024)
# CHOWN, SETUID, SETGID, DAC_OVERRIDE: file operations
# SYS_PTRACE: strace/ltrace
# Never use --privileged (gives all capabilities)
Read-Only Root: Mount the container's root filesystem as read-only. Writable paths use tmpfs or volume mounts. Prevents attackers from modifying the filesystem.

docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /var/run nginx
# --read-only makes / read-only
# Explicit --tmpfs for paths that need writes
# Volumes are still writable
User Namespaces: Map container root (UID 0) to a non-privileged host UID, so root inside the container has no special privileges on the host. Enabled via daemon.json.
Content Trust: Verify image publisher identity and image integrity using digital signatures (Docker Notary). Only signed images can be pulled or run.

export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
docker pull alpine:latest   # only pulls if signed
docker push myapp:latest    # signs and pushes
# Keys: root key, repository key, timestamp key, snapshot key
Image Scanning: Scan container images for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) in OS packages and application dependencies. Use docker scout or third-party tools.

docker scout quickview alpine:latest
docker scout cves alpine:latest
docker scout recommendations alpine:latest
# Third-party: Trivy, Snyk, Grype, Clair
# trivy image alpine:latest
Secrets Management: Never bake secrets into images. Use Docker secrets (Swarm), --secret (BuildKit build), --env-file, or dedicated tools like Vault.

# Bad: secret in image layers
# ENV DB_PASSWORD=supersecret

# Good: runtime secret
docker run -e DB_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db_pass myapp

# Better: docker secret (Swarm only)
echo "supersecret" | docker secret create db_pass -
gVisor: Container sandbox runtime (runsc) that adds a kernel between the container and the host OS, intercepting syscalls for stronger isolation.
Security Best Practices: Defense-in-depth: run non-root, read-only root, drop capabilities, enable content trust, scan images, use secrets, and avoid --privileged.

FROM node:20-slim
RUN groupadd -r app && useradd -r -g app app
USER app
COPY --chown=app:app . .

# Run command:
docker run \
  --read-only \
  --cap-drop=ALL \
  --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  --security-opt=no-new-privileges \
  --tmpfs /tmp \
  myapp

docker events: Stream real-time events from the Docker daemon: container start/stop/destroy, image pull, volume mount, network connect, etc.

docker events              # all events
docker events --filter 'type=container'
docker events --filter 'event=die' --filter 'image=nginx'
# Output: 2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z container start abc123 (image=nginx)
Prometheus Metrics: Docker daemon exposes native Prometheus metrics at /metrics endpoint. Configure in daemon.json for cluster-level monitoring with Prometheus + Grafana.
ELK Stack with Docker: Centralized logging with Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana. Containers send logs via the gelf log driver to Logstash or directly to Elasticsearch.

docker run --log-driver gelf --log-opt gelf-address=udp://logstash:12201 nginx

# docker-compose.yml for ELK
services:
  elasticsearch:
    image: docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:8.x
  logstash:
    image: docker.elastic.co/logstash/logstash:8.x
    ports: ["12201:12201/udp"]
  kibana:
    image: docker.elastic.co/kibana/kibana:8.x
    ports: ["5601:5601"]
cAdvisor: Google's cAdvisor (container advisor) exposes real-time resource usage and performance metrics per container. Often paired with Prometheus.
Resource Monitoring Deep: docker stats shows live CPU, memory, network, and disk I/O per container. Pair with --no-stream for a single snapshot.

docker stats                  # live stream
docker stats --no-stream      # single snapshot
docker stats app1 app2         # specific containers
docker stats --format "table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}"
Logging Drivers: Containers can use different log drivers: json-file (default), local (efficient compression), none (no logs), syslog, journald, fluentd, awslogs, gelf, gcplogs.
Telemetry Logs: View container STDOUT/STDERR output with docker logs. Supports tailing, timestamps, since/until filtering, and following.

docker logs app
docker logs -f app           # follow
docker logs --tail 100 app   # last 100 lines
docker logs --since 5m app   # last 5 minutes
docker logs -t app           # with timestamps

Docker in Docker: Run Docker inside a Docker container (dinD) for CI pipelines that need to build and push images. Use --privileged or mount /var/run/docker.sock.

# Mount host's Docker socket (preferred):
docker run -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock docker:24-cli build -t myapp .

# True dinD (requires --privileged):
docker run --privileged -d --name dind docker:24-dind
Caching Strategies: Speed up CI builds by caching layers. Use --cache-from to pull a previously built image and use its layers as cache. Combine with BuildKit.

# Pull cache image, then use it
# docker pull myapp:latest || true
docker buildx build \
  --cache-from=type=registry,ref=myapp:cache \
  --cache-to=type=registry,ref=myapp:cache,mode=max \
  -t myapp:latest .
Multi-Arch Builds: Build images for multiple architectures (amd64, arm64, arm/v7) simultaneously using docker buildx. Use --platform flag and push manifest lists.

docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64,linux/arm/v7 \
  -t myuser/myapp:latest \
  --push .
# Creates a single manifest list referencing all architectures
GitHub Actions with Docker: Build and push Docker images in GitHub Actions workflows. Use docker/login-action, docker/setup-buildx-action, and docker/build-push-action.

# .github/workflows/docker.yml
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
Docker Layer Caching: Preserve Docker image layers across CI runs. Use GitHub Actions cache or registry cache mounts to avoid rebuilding unchanged layers.

# GitHub Actions cache (via build-push-action)
- uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
  with:
    cache-from: type=gha
    cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

# Or inline cache in registry:
# --cache-from=type=registry,ref=myapp:cache
# --cache-to=type=registry,ref=myapp:cache,mode=max
Build Cache Optimization: Structure Dockerfiles for maximum cache reuse: install dependencies before copying source, use cache mounts for package managers.

# Cache-optimized Dockerfile
FROM node:20 AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci --only=production

FROM node:20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

FROM alpine:3.19
RUN apk add --no-cache --virtual .build-deps build-base \
    && pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt \
    && apk del .build-deps
# Also consider:
# - Combine RUN layers
# - COPY --from=builder (multi-stage)
# - .dockerignore to exclude files

Tagging Strategy: Use semantic versioning tags (1.2.3, 1.2, 1) plus descriptive tags (stable, latest, nightly). Avoid mutable tags in production; use digest pinning for immutable deployments.

# Good:
# myapp:1.2.3        specific version
# myapp:1.2           minor version (mutable)
# myapp:sha-a1b2c3d  git commit SHA
# myapp@sha256:...    pin by digest (immutable)

# Bad:
# myapp:latest        ambiguous, mutable
Non-Root User: Always run containers as a non-root user. Create a dedicated user in Dockerfile and use USER directive. This limits damage from container breaches.

FROM node:20-slim
RUN groupadd -r app && useradd -r -g app app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=app:app . .
USER app
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# At runtime also:
# docker run --user 1000:1000 ...
Read-Only Filesystem: Mount root filesystem as read-only to prevent attackers from modifying binaries or configuration. Use tmpfs for writable paths like /tmp.
Graceful Shutdown: Handle SIGTERM properly in your application so docker stop can gracefully shut down. Use dumb-init or tini for proper signal handling.

Namespaces: Linux namespaces isolate containers: pid (process tree), net (network stack), mnt (mount points), uts (hostname), ipc (SysV IPC), user (UID mapping). Docker creates one namespace set per container.
Cgroups: Control groups (cgroups) limit and account resource usage per container: CPU shares/quota, memory limit/soft limit, block I/O throttling, and PID count. Managed by containerd via cgroup v2.
OCI Spec & containerd: Docker uses containerd (high-level container runtime) which uses runc (low-level OCI runtime) to spawn containers. The OCI spec standardizes image format and runtime configuration for interoperability.
Overlay2 Storage Deep: Overlay2 layers filesystem changes using Copy-on-Write. Image layers are read-only; the container adds a writable upperdir. Reads check upperdir first, then fall through to lowerdir(s).
Veth Pairs & Bridge Forwarding: Each container gets one end of a veth pair; the other end connects to the Docker bridge (docker0). The bridge forwards traffic between containers and to the host via iptables NAT/masquerade.
iptables & NAT: Docker manages iptables rules for container networking: MASQUERADE (outbound NAT to host IP), DNAT (port publishing), FORWARD policy, and inter-container traffic isolation.

Troubleshooting Exec: Debug running containers with docker exec for shell access, process inspection, network diagnostics, and file system exploration without stopping the container.

docker exec -it web sh                     # interactive shell
docker exec web cat /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf  # read file
docker exec web ps aux                      # list processes
docker exec web netstat -tlnp               # check listening ports
docker exec web wget -qO- http://localhost/health  # test internal endpoint

// Debug container with a sidecar image (nicolaka/netshoot):
docker run -it --network container:web nicolaka/netshoot
# Now you have curl, tcpdump, nmap, iperf, dig, etc.
Dockerfile Optimization: Optimize Dockerfiles by: ordering layers from least to most frequently changing, using cache mounts, pinning base image digests, and removing build-time dependencies.

# Step 1: Pin base image by digest (immutable, no surprises):
FROM node:20-slim@sha256:<hash>

# Step 2: Install system deps before app deps:
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Step 3: Copy dependency manifests first (cache layer):
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci --only=production

# Step 4: Copy source code last (changes most often):
COPY . .

# Step 5: Remove build deps in final layer:
RUN npm cache clean --force
Multi-Stage Build Patterns: Advanced multi-stage patterns: build-target selection with --target, copying from external images, using build arguments for environment, and distroless final stages for minimal attack surface.

# build-stage produces the artifact
FROM golang:1.22 AS build-stage
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app/server

# test-stage runs unit tests (can run in CI: docker build --target test-stage)
FROM build-stage AS test-stage
RUN go test ./...

# security-stage scans for vulnerabilities
FROM aquasec/trivy:latest AS security-stage
COPY --from=build-stage /app/server /server
RUN trivy filesystem --severity CRITICAL,HIGH /server

# final: minimal distroless image
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build-stage /app/server /server
USER nonroot:nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]

# Build only the test stage:
# docker build --target test-stage -t myapp:test .
Compose Development Workflow: Use Docker Compose for local development with hot reload: mount source code as volumes, use profiles for dev services, and leverage Compose Watch for auto-restart.

services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    volumes:
      - ./src:/app/src          # live code reload (nodemon/hot reloader)
      - ./package.json:/app/package.json
    environment:
      - NODE_ENV=development
      - DB_HOST=db
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    develop:
      watch:
        - action: sync
          path: ./src
          target: /app/src
        - action: rebuild
          path: package.json

  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    ports: ["5432:5432"]
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-U", "postgres"]

  # Dev-only tools behind a profile:
  adminer:
    image: adminer
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    profiles: ["dev-tools"]

volumes:
  pgdata:

# Start: docker compose --profile dev-tools up
# Watch mode (Compose 2.22+): docker compose up --watch
Docker Build Secrets: Inject secrets at build time without baking them into image layers using BuildKit's --secret flag. Mounted as temp files only during the build step, never persisted.

# Build with a secret:
# echo "ghp_abc123" > ~/.npm-token
# docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc -t myapp .

# Dockerfile:
FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./

# Mount secret only during this RUN step (not in final image):
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc \
    npm ci --only=production

# SSH mount for private git dependencies:
# docker build --ssh default .
# RUN --mount=type=ssh pip install git+ssh://git@github.com/org/private-repo

Structured Logging: Write JSON-structured logs to STDOUT/STDERR so Docker's logging drivers can forward them to centralized systems (Elasticsearch, Loki, CloudWatch). Avoid writing logs to files inside the container.
CI/CD Pipeline Patterns: Production-grade Docker CI/CD: multi-arch builds, SBOM generation, vulnerability scanning, image signing, and atomic rollouts with health check gating.

# GitHub Actions production pipeline
jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push multi-arch image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          push: true
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
          sbom: true           # generate SBOM (Software Bill of Materials)
          provenance: true     # generate SLSA provenance

      - name: Scan image for CVEs
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
          format: sarif
          output: trivy-results.sarif
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH

      - name: Sign image with Cosign
        run: |
          cosign sign --key env://COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY \
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
Production Monitoring Stack: Monitor Docker hosts and containers in production with Prometheus + Grafana + cAdvisor + Node Exporter. Set up alerting for container restarts, OOM kills, and resource exhaustion.

services:
  cadvisor:
    image: gcr.io/cadvisor/cadvisor:latest
    volumes:
      - /:/rootfs:ro
      - /var/run:/var/run:ro
      - /sys:/sys:ro
      - /var/lib/docker:/var/lib/docker:ro
    ports: ["8080:8080"]

  node-exporter:
    image: prom/node-exporter:latest
    volumes:
      - /proc:/host/proc:ro
      - /sys:/host/sys:ro
      - /:/rootfs:ro
    command:
      - '--path.procfs=/host/proc'
      - '--path.sysfs=/host/sys'
      - '--path.rootfs=/rootfs'
    ports: ["9100:9100"]

  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:latest
    volumes:
      - ./prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
      - prometheus-data:/prometheus
    command:
      - '--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml'
      - '--storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus'

  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:latest
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    volumes:
      - grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana
    environment:
      - GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=changeme

volumes:
  prometheus-data:
  grafana-data:

# Alert on: container_oom_killed_total > 0, container_restarts > N, node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes < threshold
Backup & Disaster Recovery: Backup strategy for production Docker hosts: volume backups using temporary containers, Swarm state backup (Raft logs), image registry mirroring, and automated recovery procedures.

# 1. Backup named volumes:
docker run --rm -v myapp_data:/data -v /backup:/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/myapp_data-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz -C /data .

# 2. Backup Swarm Raft state (all manager state):
# Stop Docker, backup the Raft directory:
sudo systemctl stop docker
sudo tar czf /backup/swarm-raft-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz /var/lib/docker/swarm
sudo systemctl start docker

# 3. Periodic backup cron (host system):
# 0 2 * * * docker run --rm -v app_data:/data -v /backup:/backup alpine \
#   tar czf /backup/app_data-$(date +\%Y\%m\%d).tar.gz -C /data .

# 4. Restore a volume backup:
docker run --rm -v myapp_data:/data -v /backup:/backup alpine \
  tar xzf /backup/myapp_data-20250101.tar.gz -C /data

# 5. Mirror registry for offline/disaster recovery:
# docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --restart always --name registry registry:2
# docker pull myapp:latest && docker tag myapp:latest localhost:5000/myapp:latest && docker push localhost:5000/myapp:latest
